pharm: A phenothiazine derivative that blocks central dopamine (D2) receptors, including those in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, producing antiemetic and antipsychotic effects; it also has anticholinergic and alpha-adrenergic blocking activity.
quick: Nausea/vomiting: 5-10 mg PO 3-4x daily (max 40 mg/day in resistant cases)
May take with or without food
Not recommended except severe intractable nausea/vomiting; neonatal EPS/withdrawal risk
Phenothiazines excreted in breast milk; use caution
No specific adjustment in label; lower doses in elderly
Caution; stop if cholestatic jaundice or hepatocellular damage
Avoid - additive CNS depression; contraindicated with large amounts of CNS depressants
CBC, watch for EPS/tardive dyskinesia, NMS, BP/falls
summary: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine used for severe nausea and vomiting, schizophrenia, and short-term non-psychotic anxiety. As an antipsychotic it carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Key risks include extrapyramidal symptoms, potentially irreversible tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, blood dyscrasias, hypotension, and falls. It is contraindicated in comatose states, with large amounts of CNS depressants, and in young children/pediatric surgery.
indications: Control of severe nausea and vomiting
Short-term treatment of generalized non-psychotic anxiety (not first-line; max 20 mg/day, no longer than 12 weeks)

dosage.d: 5 mg or 10 mg tablet 3 or 4 times daily
dosage.n: Daily doses above 40 mg only in resistant cases; begin with lowest dose
Do not exceed 20 mg/day or 12 weeks (tardive dyskinesia risk)

dosage.d: Start 10 mg 3 or 4 times daily; increase gradually; usual 50-75 mg/day, severe 100-150 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase by small increments every 2-3 days
dosage.n: Longer treatment usually needed for maximal improvement

dosage.d: 20-29 lbs: 2.5 mg 1-2x/day (max 7.5 mg/day); 30-39 lbs: 2.5 mg 2-3x/day (max 10 mg/day); 40-85 lbs: 2.5 mg 3x/day or 5 mg 2x/day (max 15 mg/day)
dosage.t: Rarely more than 1 day of therapy needed
dosage.n: Not for children under 20 lbs or under 2 years; not for pediatric surgery

dosage.d: Start 2.5 mg 2-3x daily (max 10 mg day 1); ages 2-5 usually <=20 mg/day, ages 6-12 usually <=25 mg/day
dosage.n: Children more prone to extrapyramidal reactions

admin: Begin with the lowest recommended dose and titrate to individual response
Use lower doses and increase more gradually in elderly, debilitated, or emaciated patients
Keep patient lying down and observe (e.g., 30 minutes) if hypotension is a concern, especially with parenteral or large doses
Do not use in pediatric patients under 20 lbs or under 2 years, or in pediatric surgery
Discontinue at least 48 hours before myelography and do not resume for at least 24 hours after
moa: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine that blocks postsynaptic dopamine (D2) receptors in the brain. Antiemetic activity stems from D2 blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the medulla, while antipsychotic activity results from D2 blockade in mesolimbic pathways. It also exerts anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and alpha-adrenergic blocking actions, which contribute to side effects such as sedation, hypotension, and anticholinergic effects. Dopamine blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway underlies extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia, and elevation of prolactin.

absolute: Comatose states or presence of large amounts of CNS depressants (alcohol, barbiturates, narcotics)
Pediatric patients under 2 years of age or under 20 lbs
Children for conditions for which dosage has not been established
relative: Bone marrow depression or prior phenothiazine hypersensitivity (blood dyscrasias, jaundice)
Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (boxed warning - increased mortality)
Suspected Reye's syndrome or undiagnosed encephalopathy in children/adolescents
History of seizures (may lower seizure threshold)
monitor: Signs of EPS, tardive dyskinesia, and NMS
Liver function if grippe-like fever/jaundice occurs

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established; not recommended except for severe, intractable nausea and vomiting where the physician judges drug intervention is required and benefits outweigh hazards. Neonates exposed in the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder), which may require intensive care. Prolonged jaundice, EPS, and hyper/hyporeflexia have been reported in newborns of mothers who received phenothiazines.
lact: There is evidence that phenothiazines are excreted in the breast milk of nursing mothers. Caution should be exercised when prochlorperazine is administered to a nursing woman.
renal: No specific renal dosage adjustment is given. In elderly patients, the greater frequency of decreased renal (and hepatic/cardiac) function supports cautious dosing starting at the low end of the range.
hepatic: Use with caution; cholestatic jaundice has occurred. If fever with grippe-like symptoms develops, perform liver studies and stop treatment if abnormal. Elderly with decreased hepatic function should start at the low end of the dosing range.

major: CNS depressants - alcohol, anesthetics, narcotics, barbiturates (intensified/prolonged depression; contraindicated with large amounts)
Lithium - encephalopathic syndrome reported (weakness, fever, confusion, EPS, leukocytosis); monitor for neurotoxicity
moderate: Antihypertensives - guanethidine effect counteracted; thiazide diuretics may worsen orthostatic hypotension
Propranolol - increased plasma levels of both drugs
Anticonvulsants - phenothiazines may lower seizure threshold; may interfere with phenytoin (Dilantin) metabolism and precipitate toxicity
Oral anticoagulants - effect may be diminished
Epinephrine/pressor agents - reversed (paradoxical hypotension); avoid epinephrine for hypotension
minor: Drugs that lower seizure threshold should not be used with metrizamide (Amipaque)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression. Use with large amounts of CNS depressants including alcohol is contraindicated.
interactions.diagnostics: May produce false-positive phenylketonuria (PKU) test results; phenothiazines may cause false-positive pregnancy tests.

rare: Pigmentary retinopathy / corneal-lenticular deposits with prolonged high doses
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperpyrexia, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability)
Severe dystonic reaction with airway compromise

monitoring: CBC, especially first months of therapy and with pre-existing low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia
Signs of EPS, tardive dyskinesia, and NMS
Blood pressure and fall-risk assessment (especially elderly, on initiation and long term)
Liver function if grippe-like fever or jaundice develops
Periodic reassessment of need for continued therapy in long-term use
counsel: May cause drowsiness and impair alertness, especially in the first few days - avoid driving/operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating drugs
Report uncontrolled movements of the face, tongue, or limbs (possible tardive dyskinesia)
Report high fever, muscle stiffness, and confusion (possible NMS) - seek urgent care
Report sudden sore throat or signs of infection (possible low white cells)
Rise slowly to reduce dizziness/fainting; phenothiazines can increase fall risk
pk: Antipsychotic response often within 1-2 days; antiemetic effect relatively rapid orally
Not specified in label for oral tablets
Oral antiemetic effect typically several hours (IM duration up to ~12 h)
Store per product labeling at controlled room temperature
pearls: Boxed warning: increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis; not approved for this use
Cap non-psychotic anxiety use at 20 mg/day and 12 weeks to limit tardive dyskinesia risk
Antiemetic effect can mask vomiting from intestinal obstruction, brain tumor, Reye's syndrome, or chemotherapy toxicity
For drug-induced hypotension use norepinephrine or phenylephrine - NOT epinephrine (paradoxical further drop)
Children with acute illness or dehydration are especially prone to dystonic reactions
missed: If taken on a scheduled basis and a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is near the next dose; do not double up. For as-needed antiemetic use, take only when symptoms occur, within dosing limits.
overdose: Primarily extrapyramidal/dystonic reactions and CNS depression progressing to somnolence or coma; agitation, restlessness, convulsions, EKG changes, arrhythmias, fever, hypotension, dry mouth, and ileus may occur. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: maintain airway, early gastric lavage, treat EPS with antiparkinsonian agents/barbiturates/diphenhydramine, avoid inducing emesis. Do not use epinephrine for hypotension; phenothiazines are not dialyzable.
